clue.text: Dancing will get you prone with hip replacement

definitions.note: the clue gives the activity; the answer is a particular dance, a noun

indicators.note: a replacement swaps things around, so the letters are put in new places

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tongue-in-cheek warning that dancing after a hip operation will leave you flat on your back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hip replacement' reads as surgery, but 'replacement' acts on PRONE and HIP together to give HORNPIPE.
explanation.definitionFit: The hornpipe is a lively solo dance traditionally associated with sailors, so it is one kind of dancing.

clue.text: Difficult, love, to get over Everyman's coiffure

indicators.note: to get over something here is to stretch across it on both sides, so one part straddles the other

blocks.note: hard means difficult
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as I

explanation.surface: Someone tells their beloved that it is hard to get past the setter's hairstyle.
explanation.walkthrough: HARD plus O wraps around I, with the 's of 'Everyman's' read as 'is' joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A coiffure is the French-derived word for a styled arrangement of someone's hair, which is exactly a hairdo.

clue.text: Staggered, seeing fish in merlot, perhaps

indicators.note: something placed in something else ends up surrounded by it

blocks.note: an eel is a fish
merlot is an example of red wine, hence 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: Someone lurches about after finding a fish in their glass of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Merlot, perhaps' signals an example: merlot is one kind of red wine, so it gives RED.
explanation.definitionFit: To reel is to sway and stumble unsteadily, so reeled is a past-tense synonym of staggered.

clue.text: Prehistoric beast – monster – spotted, in reports

indicators.note: a report is something spoken, so the words are judged by how they sound

blocks.note: a monster is a terror, and spotted means saw; said together they make the creature's name

explanation.surface: News reports claim a prehistoric monster has been sighted, like a Loch Ness story.
explanation.walkthrough: The P is silent, so 'terror' plus 'saw' matches the sound of the creature's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Pterosaurs were flying reptiles of the dinosaur era, long extinct, so one counts as a prehistoric beast.

clue.text: In impeded light, playing game

indicators.note: playing with something means moving it around freely, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Children playing a game outside as the light fades.
explanation.walkthrough: Every letter of 'In impeded light' is used once.
explanation.definitionFit: Pig-in-the-middle is a children's ball game where one player in between tries to intercept throws.

clue.text: Holy man, righteous, flips, goes bananas

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the order runs backwards

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for saint
pure means morally righteous

explanation.surface: A saintly, virtuous man suddenly loses his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flips' looks like part of the angry picture, but it turns the saint and his purity end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Going bananas is slang for flying into a rage, and someone who erupts bursts out in sudden anger.

clue.text: Regularly fry up pieces of bread in Asia

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: Cooking instructions for frying chunks of bread somewhere in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' is slang for money, not food; the rupee is the currency of India, Pakistan and others.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread is old slang for money, and the rupee is the currency used in several South Asian countries.

clue.text: Spooner's expressed anti-Scandinavian policy as radio programming

indicators.note: Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so his way of speaking signals that swap

blocks.note: a policy against Scandinavians could be 'no Finns'; exchanging the N and F sounds gives 'fo-ninz'

explanation.surface: Spooner apparently voiced a policy against Scandinavians as if it were broadcast schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: Finland is often counted among the Nordic or Scandinavian countries, so a ban on Finns is anti-Scandinavian.
explanation.definitionFit: Phone-ins are radio shows in which listeners call the studio to speak live on air.

clue.text: Director adding touch of silliness to film's music before vacuous scene

indicators.note: a touch is a tiny amount, so only the opening letter is taken
the extra letter is added into the middle, not tacked on the end
vacuous means empty, so the inside is removed and only the ends are kept
one part comes before the other in the finished word

blocks.note: the first letter
a film's music is its score
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A film director brings a silly moment to the soundtrack ahead of an empty scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adding' here means putting in, not tacking on: the single letter goes inside the music before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Scorsese is a celebrated American film director, so he is a specific example of a director.

clue.text: If fat, side salad could make you healthy

indicators.note: making something out of materials means reshaping them, so these letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Dietary advice: an overweight person might get healthier by eating side salads.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as diet advice, but every letter of 'If fat, side salad' is reused.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'as fit as a fiddle' means in excellent physical condition, which is being healthy.

clue.text: I see diving bird returning to very cold water

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
the letter C is pronounced like the word see
a grebe is a water bird that dives for food

explanation.surface: Someone watches a diving bird come back to icy water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' gives C by its sound; no separate signal word is needed for a single letter like this.
explanation.definitionFit: An iceberg is a large floating mass of frozen water, so it is water at its very coldest.

clue.text: Poor misguided fool in the lead somewhere in Japan

indicators.note: being in the lead means being at the front, so this part comes first
misguided means steered wrongly, so the letters go astray into a new order

blocks.note: a sap is a gullible fool
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hapless, misguided fool is somehow winning a race in Japan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' looks like pity for the fool, but it is the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapporo is the largest city on the Japanese island of Hokkaido, so it is one place in Japan.

clue.text: Because of odour, eat cod only now and then

indicators.note: something happening now and then occurs at intervals, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: Because of the smell, someone eats fish only occasionally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Because of odour' looks like a single reason, but the definition is just 'Because of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Due to is a prepositional phrase meaning caused by, so it can replace because of in a sentence.

clue.text: Van is seen moving with simplicity

indicators.note: things that are moving shift position, so these letters change order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A van is spotted driving along with ease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Van' looks like a vehicle and 'moving' like driving, but they supply letters and the signal to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: Naiveness and simplicity both describe an innocent lack of worldly experience or sophistication.

clue.text: Bread boxes?

blocks.note: surface reading: containers for storing loaves in the kitchen
setter's reading: bread is slang for money, so boxes that hold and dispense money

explanation.walkthrough: Bread is old slang for money; the question mark warns that the boxes are not kitchen ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Cash machines are street-side boxes from which banks dispense money, and bread is slang for money.

clue.text: He and I sense lobby will be evacuated in an awful way

indicators.note: evacuating a building empties it, so the inside letters go and only the ends stay

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
nous is British informal for common sense
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Two people sense that a building's lobby is going to be cleared in a terrible manner.
explanation.walkthrough: Nous, rhyming with house, is a British informal word for practical good sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Heinous means shockingly wicked, so doing something heinously is acting in a dreadful, atrocious manner.

clue.text: Riotous lady, topless, drunk after sunrise

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, the time of day after the sun is up

indicators.note: riotous means wild and disorderly, so the letters are thrown into disorder
without a top, the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: taken as written
tight is informal for drunk

explanation.surface: A wild woman, topless and drunk, still partying as the sun comes up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' sits next to 'lady' but acts on the following word, so the whole of 'lady' is rearranged and 'drunk' loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Daylight is the natural light of the period between dawn and dusk, the hours that follow the sun rising.

clue.text: Primarily bubbly, a beverage your child is nowadays offered?

definitions.text: Primarily bubbly, a beverage your child is nowadays offered?

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so each word gives up its first letter

blocks.clueFragment: bubbly, a beverage your child is nowadays offered
blocks.note: the first letter of each of the eight words

explanation.surface: A frothy drink that modern parents now buy for their children in cafes.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a frothy milk drink offered to children in coffee shops these days.
explanation.definitionFit: A babycino is frothed milk, sometimes dusted with chocolate, served in cafes for small children alongside parents' coffee.

clue.text: Like Enid Blyton vis-à-vis tiny blonde?

definitions.text: Like Enid Blyton vis-à-vis tiny blonde?

blocks.clueFragment: Like Enid Blyton vis-à-vis tiny blonde?
blocks.note: surface reading: comparing a children's author with a small fair-haired person
setter's reading: the italic phrase uses exactly the letters of the author's name, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The italics mark 'tiny blonde' as a string of letters; it respells Enid Blyton, the English author of the Famous Five books.
explanation.definitionFit: Two phrases built from the same letters in different orders are said to stand in this relation to each other.

clue.text: Little Morgan trying to get support

indicators.note: only a little of the phrase is used, a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: found across the two words

explanation.surface: A small Morgan, perhaps a child, trying to get someone's backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little Morgan' looks like a nickname, but 'Little' says take only part of the words.
explanation.definitionFit: A gantry is a bridge-like overhead frame that supports cranes, signals or rail signs.

clue.text: Bit hurried

blocks.note: first meaning: gave a small sharp bite
second meaning: went somewhere quickly, as in popping to the shops

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bit' looks like a noun meaning a small piece, but it is the past tense of bite.
explanation.definitionFit: Nipped is both the past tense of a small sharp bite and British informal for going somewhere briefly and quickly.

clue.text: Earl finally – finally! – has estate ringed by 52 hedges

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the last letter of the word that follows is kept
to have something is to hold it alongside, so the parts sit together
something ringed by another thing is encircled, so it goes inside

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for earl
the italics mark the word itself as the source; its last letter
an estate is a piece of land
52 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: An earl at last owns an estate surrounded by fifty-two hedges.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'finally' is the instruction and the italic 'finally!' is the word it works on. Leylandii are fast-growing cypress trees, a notorious cause of British neighbour disputes.
explanation.definitionFit: Leylandii are fast-growing conifers planted in rows to make dense hedges, so the plural can stand for hedges.

clue.text: Pollarding allowed – that's terrible

indicators.note: pollarding a tree cuts off its top, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: lawful means allowed by law

explanation.surface: Someone is horrified that drastic pruning of trees is permitted.
explanation.walkthrough: Pollarding is a real tree-pruning practice that removes the crown, so it signals removing the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Awful and terrible are everyday synonyms, both meaning very bad or unpleasant.

clue.text: Perhaps Muscat resident will be back soon

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: in a mo, short for in a moment, means soon

explanation.surface: Someone living in Muscat promises to return shortly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a mo' is British informal for 'in a moment'. Muscat is the capital of Oman.
explanation.definitionFit: Muscat is the capital city of Oman, so someone living there is, perhaps, a citizen of Oman.

clue.text: Productive government losing power, irritating

indicators.note: losing something means it goes missing, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for government
painful can mean irksome or irritating
P is the abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A productive government that has lost its grip on power is irritating.
explanation.walkthrough: The P is removed from PAINFUL, and G stands in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Gainful means yielding profit or reward, as in gainful employment, so it means productive.

clue.text: Oddly, drew a little shrine; close to flock, highest screen displaying icons

indicators.note: oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, so the first and third letters are kept
a little is a small amount, so only the opening letter is used
the close of something is its end, so only the final letter is used

blocks.note: the first and third letters
the first letter
the last letter
top means highest

explanation.surface: Someone sketches a small shrine near a flock, while icons hang on a high screen.
explanation.walkthrough: The icons look religious beside the shrine, but they are the small pictures on a computer screen.
explanation.definitionFit: A desktop is the main screen of a computer's interface, on which program and file icons are shown.

clue.text: Provokes some toilet-roll shortages

indicators.note: some means a part of, so a run of letters is taken from inside the phrase

blocks.note: found across the words

explanation.surface: Running short of toilet paper winds people up, as in pandemic panic buying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Provokes' sits as the verb of the sentence, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To troll someone is to bait or deliberately provoke them, especially online with inflammatory comments.

clue.text: We're prepared to go back to the old you, once a little delightful innocent

indicators.note: going back is moving in the opposite direction, so the letters run backwards
a little is just a small amount, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: we'd, short for we would, says we are prepared to
ye is the old way of writing the, as in Ye Olde Tea Shoppe
ye is the archaic form of you
the first letter

explanation.surface: Someone nostalgically promises to return to the delightful innocent you once were.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old' and 'you, once' both give YE: one is the archaic spelling of the, the other the archaic you.
explanation.definitionFit: Dewy-eyed describes someone naively trusting or sentimental, so it means innocent in the sense of unworldly.
